text: 1 Introduction
crumbs: 1  Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing

title: Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing
text:
1.1 Project Background
High-performance computing (HPC) is an important part of Australia’s research infrastructure, supporting computationally intensive research across a wide range of scientific fields.
Australia has two national Tier-1 HPC facilities accessible to researchers: the National Computational Infrastructure (NCI) and the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre. Several Tier-2 HPC facilities also operate across Australian research institutions.
As research becomes increasingly data- and compute-intensive, understanding future demand for HPC resources is important for planning Australia’s national research infrastructure.
crumbs: 1  Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing

title: Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing
text:
1.2 Project Purpose
The purpose of this project is to develop a robust forecast of Australian research demand for high-performance computing to 2030.
The forecast is intended to support national policy discussions around public compute investment and future research infrastructure planning.
The project combines data engineering, descriptive analysis and forecasting using historical Australian HPC data and other indicators that may help explain changes in research compute demand.
crumbs: 1  Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing

title: Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing
text:
1.3 The Forecasting Problem
One of the main challenges is that observed HPC allocation does not necessarily represent actual research demand.
National allocation schemes operate under limited available capacity. As a result, allocated compute represents the amount of resource awarded rather than necessarily the amount researchers required.
Requested compute provides additional information about demand, but may also underestimate actual need if researchers limit their requests based on expected availability or if potential users do not apply.
The project therefore distinguishes between:

requested compute,
allocated compute,
the observed gap between requested and allocated compute, and
underlying or latent demand.
crumbs: 1  Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing

title: Forecasting Demand for National Research Supercomputing
text:
1.4 Project Objectives
The project aims to:

build a documented longitudinal dataset of Australian HPC activity,
improve comparability of compute measures across years, facilities and hardware generations,
distinguish CPU and GPU compute where possible,
examine historical demand, allocation and oversubscription,
analyse changes in Field of Research composition,
investigate potential structural drivers of HPC demand,
develop and compare suitable forecasting models,
forecast HPC demand to 2030 under different scenarios, and
estimate potential future gaps between demand and available capacity.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.1 Purpose
The first step of the project was to collect historical data on Australian HPC demand and allocation, together with other variables that may help explain changes in research compute demand over time.
The data collection focused on building a longitudinal dataset that could support both descriptive analysis and forecasting.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.2 Data Sources
Data was collected from several sources, including:

National Computational Merit Allocation Scheme (NCMAS) outcomes and supporting documentation,
National Computational Infrastructure (NCI) annual reports and publications,
Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre annual reports and publications,
Australian Research Council (ARC) funding data,
National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) funding data,
Medical Research Future Fund (MRFF) data,
research workforce and research activity data, and
Field of Research (FoR) information.

International HPC data will also be considered where suitable data is available, including information from EuroHPC, NSF ACCESS and ARCHER2.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.3 HPC Demand and Allocation Data
The main HPC dataset currently covers the period from 2013/14 to 2025/26.
The collected information includes, where available:

requested compute,
allocated compute,
facility,
HPC system,
resource type,
original compute unit,
Field of Research,
institution,
source, and
reporting period.

The level of detail varies across years because historical reporting practices and available public information are not consistent throughout the full period.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.4 Field of Research Data
Field of Research information was collected to examine how the composition of HPC use has changed over time.
Where possible, historical FoR classifications are mapped to a consistent classification to support comparison across years.
The available FoR data primarily describes the composition of allocated compute. It should therefore not automatically be interpreted as the composition of underlying research demand.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.5 Potential Demand Drivers
Additional datasets are being collected to investigate structural drivers of HPC demand.
These include research funding, workforce, research activity and other indicators that may be associated with changes in research compute requirements.
The suitability of these variables for forecasting will be assessed later based on their historical coverage, consistency and relationship with HPC demand.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.6 Data Provenance
The original source, reporting period, reported unit and relevant notes are retained wherever possible.
This allows subsequent transformations and assumptions to be traced back to the original data source and helps identify observations that may not be directly comparable across years.

title: 2  Data Collection
text:
2.7 Data Collection Limitations
The main limitations identified during data collection include:

limited consistent data before 2013,
differences in reporting formats across years,
inconsistent availability of requested and allocated compute,
incomplete separation of CPU and GPU resources in some historical data,
changes in HPC systems and accounting methods, and
differences in FoR classifications over time.

These issues are addressed in the subsequent data integration, standardisation and conversion stages.

title: 3  Potential Variable Definition
text:
3.2 HPC Demand
The main outcome of interest is Australian research demand for HPC resources.
However, demand is not directly observed in a single consistent measure. The project therefore distinguishes between several concepts.

3.2.1 Requested Compute
Requested compute represents the amount of HPC resource requested through allocation schemes where this information is available.
This provides an observable indicator of demand, but it may not represent the full level of research need if researchers limit their requests based on expected availability or if potential users do not apply.
Where possible, requested compute will be separated into:

requested CPU core-hours; and
requested GPU-hours.



3.2.2 Allocated Compute
Allocated compute represents the amount of HPC resource awarded to researchers.
Allocation is treated separately from demand because it is constrained by the amount of compute available and by the allocation process.
Where possible, allocated compute will be separated into:

allocated CPU core-hours; and
allocated GPU-hours.



3.2.3 Latent Demand
Latent demand refers to the underlying level of HPC resources that Australian researchers may require, including demand that is not fully observed through allocation or request data.
Latent demand is not directly observed and will therefore need to be estimated using available demand indicators and structural drivers.

title: 3  Potential Variable Definition
text:
3.3 Demand and Allocation Indicators
Several indicators can be derived from the historical data.
The observed request-allocation gap is defined as:
\[
\text{Request-Allocation Gap}_t =
\text{Requested Compute}_t -
\text{Allocated Compute}_t
\]
The fulfilment rate is defined as:
\[
\text{Fulfilment Rate}_t =
\frac{\text{Allocated Compute}_t}
{\text{Requested Compute}_t}
\]
These measures can help describe the relationship between observed requests and available allocation over time.
They should not automatically be interpreted as the full level of unmet demand because requested compute itself may be constrained.

title: 3  Potential Variable Definition
text:
3.4 Field of Research
Field of Research (FoR) is used to examine differences in the composition of HPC activity across research disciplines.
Potential FoR variables include:

FoR classification,
share of annual allocation by FoR,
allocated compute by FoR, and
changes in FoR composition over time.

The currently available FoR information primarily represents allocation rather than directly observed requested demand. Any use of allocation composition as a proxy for demand composition will therefore be documented as an assumption.

title: 3  Potential Variable Definition
text:
3.5 Potential Structural Drivers
The project will investigate variables that may help explain changes in HPC demand over time.
Potential drivers include:

3.5.1 Research Funding

Australian Research Council (ARC) funding,
National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) funding,
Medical Research Future Fund (MRFF) funding, and
broader research and development expenditure where suitable data is available.



3.5.2 Research Workforce and Activity

research workforce size,
number of researchers,
PhD completions,
number of research projects, and
grant activity in compute-intensive research fields.



3.5.3 Compute Intensity
Potential indicators of changing compute intensity include:

compute use per project,
compute use by Field of Research,
changes in CPU and GPU use, and
changes associated with increasingly compute-intensive research.



3.5.4 HPC Infrastructure
Infrastructure variables may include:

available HPC systems,
system commissioning and retirement,
available CPU and GPU resources, and
changes in national compute capacity.

These variables are important for distinguishing changes in demand from changes caused by additional supply.

title: 3  Potential Variable Definition
text:
3.6 International Benchmarking Variables
Where suitable data is available, international HPC systems may be used as external benchmarks.
Potential indicators include:

compute per researcher,
compute per research dollar,
allocation and utilisation, and
changes in CPU and GPU use.

Potential international comparators include EuroHPC, NSF ACCESS and ARCHER2.

title: 3  Potential Variable Definition
text:
3.7 Variable Selection for Modelling
Not all potential variables will necessarily be included in the final forecasting model.
Variable selection will consider:

theoretical relevance to HPC demand,
historical data coverage,
consistency of measurement,
availability through the forecast horizon,
relationship with observed HPC demand, and
the limited number of annual observations available for modelling.

The final model will prioritise a small number of interpretable variables rather than including a large number of predictors in a short annual time series.
